newsitem.title: USA: U.S. punishes Colombia over drugs for second year.
newsitem.headline: U.S. punishes Colombia over drugs for second year.

text.p: The United States, citing "rampant corruption" at top levels of the Colombian government, announced on Friday it was again denying Bogota certification as an ally in the fight against drugs.
It was the second consecutive year that Colombia was included on a list of states that had failed to cooperate fully in global anti-drug efforts.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, announcing President Bill Clinton's decision, said it was "the result of our concern that corruption remains rampant at the highest levels of the Colombian government, and that senior officials are failing to cooperate with us in the fight against drugs."
The United States says that Colombia accounts for about three quarters of the cocaine entering the United States and is also a leading supplier of heroin.

Washington charges that President Ernesto Samper not only accepted but solicited over $6 million from Colombian drug traffickers to finance his 1994 presidential campaign. Last year it revoked Samper's U.S. visa.
Samper was absolved by the Colombian Congress last year of any wrongdoing in connection with his campaign finances.

Clinton's decision to deny Colombia certification put it in the same bracket as Afghanistan, Burma, Iran, Nigeria and Syria. The annual certification exercise, which covers 32 countries, is required by the U.S. Congress.

In Bogota, the Colombian government strongly criticised the U.S. decision. Vice President Carlos Lemos Simmonds called it "arbitrary and unjust" and said it threatened to drive U.S.-Colombian relations to a new low. He said certification had lost all credibility.
The decision means that Colombia will continue to be denied U.S. government loans and face U.S. opposition to loans by the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.
But U.S. officials said they would seek ways to ensure that anti-drug aid reached Colombia and gave no sign they would apply trade sanctions against Colombia.

Albright said the decision was "in no way ... meant to undercut the valiant and effective efforts of those Colombians who are fighting on the front lines against the drug trade." She said Clinton wanted to limit the impact on U.S. businesses and the Colombian police and military.

Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard said Colombia's private sector had played an important role in urging the government to act against narcotics and mentioned in particular the flower growers' association and the bankers' association.
"We strongly want to recognise that and take all that into account," Gelbard told reporters.
Gelbard charged, however, that Samper "took action on key certification objectives only at the final hour, when it was clear that rhetoric alone would not suffice".

He said Colombia's coca crop had expanded by 32 percent, that the country was "far and away the largest producer of cocaine," that seizures of drugs had dropped and that more heroin was available than ever before. "Virtually all of that heroin is destined for the United States," he said.

"Colombian government inaction" had allowed Cali Cartel drug kings to operate their businesses from jail, and its leaders, the Rodriguez-Orejuela brothers, faced only relatively short prison sentences, he said.
Gelbard held out one incentive to Colombia, saying that "adequate progress" in fighting drugs could justify re-certification this year in U.S. national interests, as permitted by U.S. law.
